title: Equivalent forms of a relationship

worked_examples.q: Double an input, then add 3. Write the rule and find the output at x=4.
states: The input is doubled then three is added

steps.title: Trace the first verb
steps.action: Attach times two to the input x.
steps.narration: Double the input before adding anything.

steps.title: Trace the second verb
steps.action: Attach plus three to the doubled input.
steps.narration: The full output is two x plus three.

steps.title: Test the rule
steps.action: Substitute four and evaluate.
steps.narration: Four becomes eight then eleven.

worked_examples.repair: Place a value between the double and add arrows.

worked_examples.q: A table has 0→5, 1→6, 2→7. State a rule that fits and show its flow for input 2.
states: Three given rows rise by one per input step
At zero the output is five
Input two plus five gives seven

steps.title: Compare equal input steps
steps.action: Each input increase of one matches an output increase of one.
steps.narration: A simple add-five rule is a candidate.

steps.title: Use input zero
steps.action: Five is the output when input is zero.
steps.narration: This is the fixed part of the candidate rule.

steps.title: Draw a flow
steps.action: Send two through plus five to get seven.
steps.narration: The flow reproduces the stated row.

worked_examples.verify: The candidate gives 5,6,7 on all stated inputs; other rules may fit only these rows.
worked_examples.misconception: Claiming the three rows uniquely prove a rule for every input.
worked_examples.repair: Call it a fitting rule and check every given row.

worked_examples.q: The flow adds 2 then triples. Write its formula and output at x=1.

steps.title: Preserve the intermediate
steps.action: Write x plus two in a single bracket.
steps.narration: The second arrow acts on the complete result.

steps.title: Build formula
steps.action: Multiply the complete bracket by three.
steps.narration: The flow is three times the quantity x plus two.

steps.title: Show equivalent expression
steps.action: Multiply each term inside the bracket by three.
steps.narration: This gives three x plus six.

steps.title: Check with an input
steps.action: At one the bracket is three, then triples to nine.
steps.narration: Both formula forms agree.

worked_examples.misconception: Writing 3x+2 applies the triple to x alone.
worked_examples.repair: Keep the entire intermediate result inside brackets.

worked_examples.q: Rule A doubles x then adds 3. Rule B adds 3 then doubles. Are they equivalent? Use x=2.
states: Two flows start at the same input two
Seven differs from ten, so the rules differ

steps.title: Follow A in order
steps.action: Double two then add three to get seven.
steps.narration: Keep A in its own lane.

steps.title: Follow B in order
steps.action: Add three then double to get ten.
steps.narration: Do not use A’s intermediate value.

steps.title: Compare shared input
steps.action: Seven is different from ten.
steps.narration: One counterexample proves that the rules are not equivalent.

worked_examples.misconception: Treating addition and multiplication as interchangeable in a flow.
worked_examples.repair: Use one common input in two separate lanes.

worked_examples.skill: Choose a formula from a table
worked_examples.q: The rows are 0→4,1→6,2→8. Which fits: A: y=2x+4 or B: y=4x+2? Check all rows.
worked_examples.answer: A fits every row; B fails already at x=0.

model.description: Choose a formula from a table

steps.title: Evaluate A row by row
steps.action: Compute two x plus four at zero, one and two.
steps.narration: Each calculated output matches the stated row.

steps.title: Find B’s first mismatch
steps.action: At zero, four times zero plus two is two.
steps.narration: The table says four, so B is ruled out.

steps.title: State the conclusion
steps.action: A matches every supplied row while B fails one.
steps.narration: The comparison concerns these two candidates on the given rows.

worked_examples.misconception: Comparing only the multiplier without testing the fixed value.

worked_examples.q: “Start at 5 and subtract twice the input.” Write a formula and find its output at x=−1.
states: The start is five; twice x is subtracted

steps.title: Name the repeated quantity
steps.action: Twice x means two multiplied by x.
steps.narration: Keep the factor with the variable.

steps.title: Write the full rule
steps.action: Subtract the whole two x from five.
steps.narration: The order is five minus two x.

steps.title: Substitute with brackets
steps.action: Twice negative one is negative two; subtracting it gives seven.
steps.narration: Check the sign before simplifying.

worked_examples.repair: Place the five before the subtraction arrow.

worked_examples.q: A flow gives y=3(x−2). A classmate writes y=3x−6. Show why these are the same rule for every x.
worked_examples.answer: 3(x−2)=3x−6 by distribution, so they agree for every x.

steps.title: Mark the first product
steps.action: Three multiplies x to produce three x.
steps.narration: The outside factor applies to every bracket term.

steps.title: Mark the signed product
steps.action: Three times negative two is negative six.
steps.narration: Keep the negative sign in the second product.

steps.title: Compare expressions
steps.action: The expanded form is exactly the second expression.
steps.narration: An identity proves equivalence for all inputs in the common domain.

worked_examples.verify: At any x, distribution gives 3x−6; both have the same domain.
worked_examples.misconception: Expanding only the first bracket term.
worked_examples.repair: Draw a multiplication arrow from three to each term.

worked_examples.q: Compare “half the input then add 4” with “add 4 then halve”. Are they equivalent? Use x=8.
states: Use input eight in both flows

steps.title: Trace the first wording
steps.action: Half eight to four and then add four.
steps.narration: A gives eight.

steps.title: Trace the second wording
steps.action: Add four to eight first and halve twelve.
steps.narration: B gives six.

steps.title: Compare the outputs
steps.action: Eight and six are different.
steps.narration: The bracket placement changes which total is halved.

worked_examples.misconception: Assuming both descriptions halve only x.
worked_examples.repair: Draw each operation order and bracket the intermediate total.

worked_examples.q: An activity charges R15 once plus R4 per ticket. Give C(n), a table at n=0,1,3, and sensible inputs.
worked_examples.answer: C(n)=15+4n rand; 0→R15,1→R19,3→R27; n a whole number ≥0.
states: Fixed fifteen plus four per ticket
Ticket counts are nonnegative whole numbers

steps.title: Build the repeated part
steps.action: Count four rand once for each ticket.
steps.narration: Four n changes when n changes.

steps.title: Add the once-only charge
steps.action: Keep fifteen outside the repeated amount.
steps.narration: The formula is fifteen plus four n.

steps.title: Fill each row
steps.action: Evaluate zero, one and three tickets.
steps.narration: Each table output follows the same rule.

steps.title: Check the context domain
steps.action: A ticket count cannot be fractional or negative.
steps.narration: Domain affects which symbolic inputs make sense.

worked_examples.misconception: Charging R15 per ticket or allowing negative ticket counts.

worked_examples.skill: Area as flow and expanded formula
worked_examples.q: A rectangle has width 3 cm and length (x+2) cm. Write area as a flow and two equivalent formulas. Find area at x=5.
worked_examples.answer: A=3(x+2)=3x+6 cm²; when x=5, A=21 cm².

model.description: Area as flow and expanded formula

states: Flow: add 2 to x, then multiply by 3

steps.title: Follow the length first
steps.action: Add two to x to obtain the whole length.
steps.narration: The width does not add to the length.

steps.title: Build area product
steps.action: Multiply the whole length by width three.
steps.narration: Area is width times length.

steps.title: Split the area
steps.action: Three multiplies x and two, giving three x plus six.
steps.narration: The two forms represent the same rectangle.

steps.title: Check dimension
steps.action: At five, length is seven and width three.
steps.narration: Area twenty one has square centimetre units.

worked_examples.misconception: Adding 3 and x+2 rather than multiplying side lengths.
worked_examples.repair: Show the full rectangle as two adjoining regions.

worked_examples.q: A table contains 0→0 and 2→4. Both y=2x and y=x² fit. Show they are not the same rule.
worked_examples.answer: At x=1, 2x=2 but x²=1, so they are not equivalent.
states: Two rows agree with both proposed rules

steps.title: Choose a fresh input
steps.action: Test one, which the table does not show.
steps.narration: Agreement at finitely many rows alone cannot prove equivalence.

steps.title: Evaluate both rules
steps.action: Twice one is two; one squared is one.
steps.narration: The candidates differ on the same input.

steps.title: Use the counterexample
steps.action: Two differs from one.
steps.narration: The rules are not identical, even though both fit the displayed rows.

worked_examples.verify: Both fit x=0,2; at x=1 outputs 2 and 1 differ.
worked_examples.misconception: Claiming a few matched table rows prove two formulas identical.
worked_examples.repair: Look for a fresh input or prove an identity.

worked_examples.q: A complete carton contains 6 eggs. Are “six times the number of cartons” and E(c)=6c equivalent for c=0,1,2,…? Could c=−1 describe the situation?
worked_examples.answer: Yes on nonnegative whole-number c; c=−1 is outside the context.
states: Each complete carton contributes six eggs
The descriptions agree for every valid whole c
A negative carton count is invalid here

steps.title: Build the equal groups
steps.action: Multiply the number of cartons by six eggs each.
steps.narration: This translates the words into a formula.

steps.title: Test sample rows
steps.action: At zero, one and two cartons count zero, six and twelve eggs.
steps.narration: The samples illustrate the translation.

steps.title: State the identity
steps.action: For each valid carton count, both descriptions mean six c.
steps.narration: The same operation, not just the samples, justifies equivalence.

steps.title: Restrict the domain
steps.action: A negative complete-carton count is not a situation in this question.
steps.narration: Keep the context with the algebra.

worked_examples.verify: Both descriptions are 6c eggs for c∈{0,1,2,…}; −1 is not a valid count.
worked_examples.misconception: Declaring every algebraic input a possible physical count.
worked_examples.repair: Mark the allowed carton inputs on a number line.

worked_examples.q: A plan charges R8 once and R3 per visit. Compare A(n)=8+3n with B(n)=3(n+8) using n=0 and n=4. Which represents the plan?
worked_examples.answer: A represents it: A(0)=R8,A(4)=R20. B(0)=R24,B(4)=R36, so B does not.
states: A once-only eight-rand charge plus three per visit
At zero visits, actual cost is eight
B(4)=36; only A models this plan

steps.title: Read the starting amount
steps.action: With no visits, the only cost is eight rand.
steps.narration: Zero is a powerful test for a fixed fee.

steps.title: Test zero in both formulas
steps.action: A gives eight while B incorrectly gives twenty four.
steps.narration: The bracket multiplies the fixed charge.

steps.title: Check the first candidate again
steps.action: At four visits, eight plus twelve is twenty rand.
steps.narration: A repeats only the per-visit charge.

steps.title: Check the other candidate
steps.action: B makes three times twelve equal thirty six.
steps.narration: The extra amount confirms that B models a different arrangement.

worked_examples.verify: The words imply 8+3n; at n=0 and n=4 A gives 8,20, while B gives 24,36.
worked_examples.misconception: Multiplying a once-only fee by the number of visits.
worked_examples.repair: Put the fixed fee outside the multiplication bracket.

worked_examples.q: Outputs 3,5,7 correspond to inputs 0,1,2. Compare A(x)=2x+3 and B(x)=3x+2; give the matching candidate and explain.
worked_examples.answer: A matches all three rows; B(0)=2≠3 and B(2)=8≠7.
states: Only A matches every stated row

steps.title: Evaluate A at each input
steps.action: Calculate two x plus three at zero, one and two.
steps.narration: All outputs agree with the table.

steps.title: Test B at zero
steps.action: Three times zero plus two is two, not three.
steps.narration: One mismatch rules B out.

steps.title: Test B at two
steps.action: Three times two plus two is eight, not seven.
steps.narration: The middle row alone was misleading.

steps.title: Conclude precisely
steps.action: A is the matching candidate among the two proposed rules.
steps.narration: A short table does not establish uniqueness among all possible formulas.

worked_examples.misconception: Trusting one matching row instead of checking every row.
worked_examples.repair: Highlight the first and third mismatches.

worked_examples.skill: Identity versus counterexample in one scene
worked_examples.q: Compare A(x)=2(x+5), B(x)=2x+10, C(x)=2x+5. Which are equivalent for every x? Show outputs at x=0 and x=3.
worked_examples.answer: A and B are equivalent for every x; C differs. At x=0: 10,10,5; x=3: 16,16,11.

model.description: Identity versus counterexample in one scene

states: A and B agree for all x; C fails

steps.title: Expand both bracket parts
steps.action: Distribute two to x and five.
steps.narration: The whole bracket is doubled.

steps.title: Compare symbolic forms
steps.action: Expanded A is exactly B.
steps.narration: An identity proves these two agree for all x.

steps.title: Test a counterexample
steps.action: At zero A and B give ten; C gives five.
steps.narration: One input disproves equivalence with C.

steps.title: Check another input
steps.action: At three A and B give sixteen; C gives eleven.
steps.narration: The two results stay distinct.

steps.title: State the exact conclusion
steps.action: A and B are equivalent, while C is not.
steps.narration: Sample checks illustrate the algebraic identity and counterexample.

worked_examples.verify: 2(x+5)=2x+10 identically; at zero and three C differs.
worked_examples.misconception: Assuming 2(x+5)=2x+5 by distributing to only x.
worked_examples.repair: Draw one distribution arrow to each bracket term.

practice_questions: “Triple x then subtract 1.” Write a formula.
Three times x less one is 3x−1.
Table 0→2,1→3,2→4. Give one fitting simple rule.
x+2 agrees with every listed row; it is a fitting candidate.
Flow adds 4 then doubles. Give a formula.
At x=2 compare 3x+1 with 3(x+1). Are they equivalent?
No; at x=2 they give 7 and 9.
Try the same input in both.
At zero the expected output is six, not two.
“Start at 7 and subtract twice x.” Formula and output at x=−1?
Are 4(x−3) and 4x−12 equivalent for all x?
Half x then add 3 versus add 3 then halve. Compare at x=6.
First gives 6; second gives 4.5; not equivalent.
R12 once plus R5 per ticket. Give C(n), C(0), C(2), and sensible n.
C(n)=12+5n; C(0)=R12; C(2)=R22; n a whole number ≥0.
The table 0→0,2→8 fits y=4x and y=2x². Find an input where they disagree.
Choose an input not in the table.
Rectangle width 4, length x+3. Give equivalent area formulas and area at x=2.
A=4(x+3)=4x+12; at x=2, A=20 square units.
A=R5+R4 per visit; B=R4(n+5). Which reflects the stated fixed R5 at zero visits?
The once-only five is not multiplied by four.
Table 0→2,1→5,2→8. Compare 3x+2 and 2x+3 on all rows.
Compare 3(x+2), 3x+6 and 3x+2 for all x; give outputs at x=0.
First two equivalent for all x; at zero they give 6 and 6, while third gives 2.
mastery_questions: “Double x, then subtract five.” Give a formula and output at x=4.
y=2x−5; output 3.
Two times four minus five equals three.
Table 0→3,1→7,2→11. Compare y=4x+3 and y=3x+4. Which fits?
y=4x+3 fits; y=3x+4 fails at x=0 and x=2.
First gives 3,7,11; second gives 4,7,10.
Are 5(x−2) and 5x−10 equivalent for every x? Explain and evaluate both at x=3.
Yes; 5(x−2)=5x−10, and both give 5 at x=3.
Distribute five to x and negative two; x=3 gives five.
A workshop charges R20 once plus R3 per item. Give C(n), costs at zero and four, sensible n, and reject 3(n+20).
C(n)=20+3n; C(0)=R20; C(4)=R32; n whole ≥0; 3(n+20) gives R60 at zero, so it is wrong.
The fixed fee occurs once and the per-item fee repeats.
A=2(x+4), B=2x+8 and C=2x+4. Identify the equivalent pair for all x, use x=0 to reject the third, and give outputs at x=3.
A and B equivalent for all x; at x=0 A=B=8 but C=4; at x=3 A=B=14 and C=10.
Distribute two to x and four to prove A=B. The counterexample at zero rejects C.
reassessment_questions: “Triple x then add five” and “add five then triple”. At x=2 compare outputs.
Are 4(x−2) and 4x−8 equivalent for every x? Give a reason.
Four multiplies both x and negative two.
A booking costs R9 once plus R2 per seat. Give the formula, table for zero and three seats, and sensible seat counts.
Count the fixed R9 once; three seats add R6.
